title: Lesson 83: Advising the Business: Translating Architecture into ROI and a Roadmap
description: Three applied questions on translating a Salesforce architecture into a fundable business case: which costs belong in the total cost of ownership model, how a phased ramp changes payback and net present value, and how sequencing decisions and sponsor communication decide whether the programme stays funded.

questions.question: An architect presents a five-year case for a distribution programme. The model lists licences, implementation, operations, maintenance, integration, and change, and projects net annual value of 240,000 at run rate. A challenge comes back that the case is too optimistic. Applying the lesson's cost model, what is the most likely gap in the model?
options: The model is complete, because the six direct cost lines are the full set of costs a Salesforce solution creates.

The model omits indirect costs, which the lesson says often exceed direct costs for mature implementations: organizational costs including the opportunity cost of maintenance capacity, technical debt interest, governance overhead, and the cost of functionality that is implemented but never adopted.
The model overstates the licence line, which should always be modelled as zero because platform licences are covered by the base platform.
The model should drop maintenance, because enhancement and release adaptation fall under the implementation line as one-time cost.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates TCO into six direct lines (licence and consumption, implementation, operational, maintenance, integration, change) and four indirect categories (organizational costs, technical debt interest, governance overhead, unused functionality), and notes that indirect costs are real but easy to overlook and often exceed direct costs for mature implementations. Maintenance is described as typically consuming 60 to 80 percent of development capacity on mature solutions, so it is the largest ongoing category, not a one-time line.

questions.question: The same programme has a one-time cost of 520,000 and net annual value of 240,000 at run rate, which gives a simple payback of 2.2 years. The phased ramp shows year 1 net of negative 65,000, year 2 net of positive 185,000, and cumulative cash turning positive early in year 4, with a five-year net present value of approximately 67,000 against an undiscounted five-year net of 320,000. What does the lesson say this difference means for the architect?
options: The simple payback figure is the honest number and the ramp table should be removed from the sponsor pack, because it only creates doubt.
The gap means the discount rate should be lowered until the net present value matches the undiscounted figure, so the two numbers agree.

Steady state does not arrive on day one, most value lands in years 4 and 5 and discounting punishes that shape, so the most valuable thing the architecture can do is move value earlier; sequencing is therefore a financial instrument and each month of Phase 1 slip carries a cost of delay.
The net present value is irrelevant because payback period already accounts for the time value of money, so only the 2.2 year figure needs to be presented.
questions.explanation: The lesson shows the ramp and cumulative table precisely to make this point: the steady-state net is 240,000 a year and simple payback is 2.2 years, but cumulative cash turns positive only early in year 4 because Phase 1 delivers half a year of benefit and Phase 2 lands mid-year 2. It states that the single most valuable thing the architecture can do is move value out of year 2 and into year 1, that sequencing decides the cash curve, and that the cost of delay during the ramp is roughly 46,000 of net value per month. Payback period ignores the time value of money, which is why it flatters long programmes without the ramp shown.

questions.question: A sponsor asks two questions in the same meeting: whether the programme can be delivered cheaper, and whether it can be delivered faster. The architect has a per-month net value figure for the ramp and a named list of lower-value scope. Which pair of responses follows the lesson?
options: Answer the cost question with a promise to find savings during delivery, and answer the speed question by agreeing to compress the schedule so the sponsor stays positive about the programme.

Answer the cost question with scope rather than price by showing the specific cut, the value lines it moves, and the new payback; answer the speed question with the per-month cost of delay so acceleration becomes a decision with arithmetic attached.
Answer both questions by presenting a menu of options without a recommendation, so the sponsor chooses the tradeoff themselves.
Answer both questions by lowering the assumed value lines so the case looks more conservative, then re-present the same plan.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that the answer to cheaper is scope, not price, and that the architect should show the specific cut, the value lines it moves, and the new payback, because a sponsor who hears what a cut costs is making an informed trade. It states that the answer to faster is a cost-of-delay question, answered with the per-month value figure already calculated so the sponsor can decide rather than being managed. It also warns against presenting a menu of options without a recommendation, since that softens a recommendation into a list.
